# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it through and checked the arithmetic.
- **24-month per-hour gains:** 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8% on timesheets, and 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5% on system logs.
- **Halden continuers:** 96.8/86.6 gives +11.8%, and 34.9/40.3 is a fall of 13.4%.
- **Mediation shares:** these add to 100%.
- **Meetings:** the change in treated offices compared with control is −3.3 hours. That matches the nine-month figure, and there is now a real baseline (7.4 in treated offices, 7.2 in control).

## What the report says

This is the Varden team, now joined by a Halden author, reporting 24-month follow-up.

**Varden case-processing offices** stayed randomised for two years. A stricter hours measure was added: active log-in time on the case system.
- The per-hour gain relative to control is +9.8% on timesheets and **+8.5% on logs (CI 3.4 to 13.8)**, against +12.5% at nine months.
- Output per employee is −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2).
- Quality, sick days and resignations are about where they were at nine months.
- A mediation analysis registered at month 11 attributes **47% of the gain to fewer meetings** and 18% to reduced fatigue. The remaining 35% is unexplained.
- Two control offices cut their meetings on their own initiative. Their output per hour then rose about 4%, but there was no comparison for them, and the authors say so.

**The counter arm was ended at month 12.** Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control, and restoring service would have needed 12% more staff, at about 9% more cost per contact.

**Halden subset:** 14 of the 23 organisations with output records responded.
- **Reverted:** 3, with output at 88–91 at the point of reversion.
- **Continued:** 11. Their per-hour gain is +11.8%, which the authors present as an upper bound for organisations that choose to continue.

**On the earlier papers:** the "entirely an artifact" claim fails against a test that meets the re-analysis's own standards. The meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, so they could not show whether effects decay.

## Overall assessment

This is the strongest document in the set, and it settles several of the questions the earlier papers left open. It:
- registered its follow-up analyses before seeing the results,
- added a stricter hours measure even though it shrank their own estimate,
- reported the decline in the gain, and
- kept the unplanned observation clearly labelled.

The section on the earlier papers is fair to both. It credits the re-analysis on measurement and corrects it on its conclusion.

## Inconsistencies and overstatements

**1. The Summary mixes hours measures when describing the decline.** "Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" compares a timesheet figure with a log figure. The like-for-like comparison, which the body itself calls the right one, is **12.5% to 9.8%**. This errs in the conservative direction, but it overstates the decline by about half.

**2. The decline itself is not established.** The nine-month and 24-month intervals overlap heavily (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2). The body's phrase, "consistent with some fading", is right. The Summary's "the gain has therefore declined" states as fact what is only a point-estimate drop. Reporting the change with its own confidence interval would settle the wording. What *is* established is that a gain remains at 24 months.

**3. "Confirms" is stronger than "survives".** The registered test does count, and the pathway held up. However:
- It uses the same seven treated offices that generated the hypothesis.
- If the 24-month analysis includes months 1–9, it partly re-tests the original data.
- "A larger sample of office-months" adds observations within those offices, not independent units. There are still 14 clusters, so the earlier concern about few clusters applies to the 28–66% interval.
- Meeting reductions were not randomised, so the mediator–outcome link depends on assumptions. The Limitations section acknowledges this.

"Supported by a registered test in the same offices" is the accurate claim. Independent confirmation needs other sites.

**4. What do log-in hours include?** If staff in meetings aren't logged into the case system, meeting time is already largely excluded from the "output per log-measured hour" denominator. In that case, cutting meetings can't raise the outcome simply by shrinking the denominator. The 47% would then mean something more like "fewer meetings made case time more productive", for example through longer uninterrupted blocks. That is a different mechanism from "low-value time was removed", and the report should say which applies.

**5. The Halden reversions don't all fit the stated pattern.** The Summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency, however, is discretionary work by every coding used in this literature, and it cited client deadlines, not coverage. That is a genuine counter-example within discretionary work, and it shouldn't be absorbed into the coverage story. Also, the nine organisations that declined to provide data may differ from responders, probably in the unfavourable direction.

## Gaps worth filling, since the data exist

**6. Backlog.** A sustained −3.4% output per employee accumulates. If control offices are just keeping up with incoming cases, treated offices fall roughly 0.8 months of output behind over two years. The case-management system can report queue size and time to decision. Given statutory deadlines, this is the service measure that matters for case-processing, just as waiting time was for counters.

**7. Cost per case.** The report costs the counter arm (+9% per contact) but not the arm that continued. Case-processing staff still work about 8% above scheduled hours, probably as paid overtime, while output per employee is slightly down. For the county's decision, cost per case closed is the key figure.

**8. The meeting-audit offices can be compared with other control offices.** The report compares the two control offices that cut meetings only with their own previous six months. Comparing them with the other five control offices over the same period would remove seasonality and trend. It would also show how much their change pulled the control arm toward the treated arm after month 15. That effect would make the trial's estimate after month 15 conservative.

## Correcting my earlier estimate

In my reading of the nine-month report, I estimated that "most of the 12.5% per-hour gain is compatible with simply removing time that produced no cases". That figure was a rough accounting calculation. It treated meeting hours as producing no output and assumed treated offices started at the control level of meetings. The registered estimate is **47% (28–66%)**. So "most" sits at the top of that interval, and the 47% figure should replace my estimate. Meetings are a major pathway, roughly half, not the whole story. The unexplained 35% is a real gap.

## The picture across all five documents

- **Now settled (one public employer, randomised, best available measurement):**
  - A per-hour gain of about 8–10% remains at 24 months in discretionary work. The claim that the gain is "entirely an artifact" is refuted for this setting.
  - The meta-analysis's "no sign of decay" claim is withdrawn on the evidence: its long-follow-up studies could not test for decay.
  - **Coverage-bound work:** keeping opening hours unchanged degraded service, and restoring it raises cost. The county ended this arm, and Halden's reversions point the same way.
  - Cutting meetings is a substantial pathway, roughly half of the gain. Fatigue contributes less.
- **Supported, not yet settled:** output per employee in discretionary work falls about 0–4%. Whether the per-hour gain fades a little or stabilises is unknown; the point estimate dropped, but the drop is within noise.
- **Open:**
  - Whether reorganisation alone can capture most of the gain. The authors rightly say their trial cannot answer this. A trial with a reorganise-only arm would.
  - Whether these results hold outside one public employer.
  - What makes up the unexplained third of the gain.
  - Backlog and cost for the case-processing arm.

I can draft a referee report on this follow-up, or update the evidence summary to cover all five documents.
